claims.text: The dynamic mechanical response of solidified FeNiCrMn is controlled by a temperature- and strain-rate-dependent transition in dislocation mobility.
At moderate temperature and strain-rate conditions, thermally activated dislocation glide dominates deformation in FeNiCrMn.
Thermally activated dislocation glide produces a balanced strength-ductility response in FeNiCrMn.
At low temperatures or high strain rates, reduced thermally assisted dislocation motion leads to dislocation drag or localized stress concentrations.
Dislocation drag or localized stress concentrations increase apparent yield strength while limiting ductility.
Atomic-scale chemical inhomogeneity is inherent in solidified FeNiCrMn.
Atomic-scale chemical inhomogeneity creates a distribution of local activation energies for dislocation motion.
At higher temperatures and lower strain rates, dislocations overcome local barriers by thermal activation, maintaining ductility.
At lower temperatures or higher strain rates, insufficient thermal activation causes dislocation drag or stress localization.
Low-temperature or high-strain-rate tests will exhibit higher yield and flow stresses than the moderate-temperature, low-rate baseline.
Low-temperature or high-strain-rate tests will exhibit reduced uniform elongation.
Elevated temperatures or low strain rates will produce lower strength and greater ductility.
A consistent transition in the temperature-strain-rate plane would support dislocation mobility as the governing mediator.
The proposed mechanism applies only while FeNiCrMn remains in the same phase and microstructural state and while twinning, cracking, or phase transformations do not dominate.
Deformation twinning or adiabatic shear banding may become active under extreme loading and invalidate the proposed mechanism.
The transition can be tested by varying temperature from approximately 250 to 350 K and strain rate from 10^-3 to 10^3 s^-1 while holding the initial microstructure consistent.

The hypothesis would be falsified if strength-ductility changes fail to correlate systematically with dislocation mobility or if another deformation mechanism dominates without evidence of a dislocation-drag transition.
